transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-09-08 14:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Patel (Redwood SE), Liam Park (Redwood CSM) — Sara Hughes (Head of ML, RiverGrid), Diego Ramos (Infra), Priya Nair (SRE), Alex Kim (Product)
Links shared: pilot-run-results.csv (drive link), burst-capacity-options.pdf (redwood link), security-FAQ.pdf

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Quick review of last week's throughput numbers; median token/s improved after K V cache warmup but tail latencies persist.
- Agreed to run batch/concurrency sweep and a focused lab to reproduce queue spikes.
- Priorities: reduce 95/99th latency, verify steady-state throughput at target concurrency, test burst fallback behavior.

Topics:
- Continuous batching behavior and warmup
- Concurrency targets and queue shaping
- Queueing/backpressure and fallback model variants
- Telemetry required for lab reproduction

Action items (quick):
- Owen: run batch-sweep, share CSV
- Diego: provide traces
- Maya: send pricing + contract addendum

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, uh trying to keep to 30 minutes, we did 42 but ok.
[00:22] Sara: yep, thanks Maya, we have Diego and Priya on to help with infra bits, Alex will jump in near the end.
[00:38] Maya: awesome, quick agenda — recap last run, discuss the queue spikes, decide next steps for lab. Owen you want to kick off with the numbers?
[00:53] Owen: sure, yeah. so from last week's sweep, we saw that continuous batching improved tokens per second by roughly 1.8x at mid concurrency once K V cache warmed. but the 95th and 99th latencies still hang around due to occasional queue head-of-line stalls.
[01:20] Diego: when you say K V cache warmed, do you mean per-connection KV or shared across the pod? we're on a mix of sticky sessions.
[01:32] Owen: good call — it's per-worker KV cache with TTL 5 minutes; sticky sessions amplify warm-cache effects for that connection. we think for your shape (lots of short multi-turns) the cache helps after about 40 to 60 requests per session.
[01:52] Priya: right, our traffic is a long-tail; many users have spikes of 5 to 20 calls, not long sessions. so warmup is spotty.
[02:05] Sara: and we saw a couple of 800–1200ms spikes when concurrency hit 40. our target is to be under 200ms p50 and under 800ms p95 for interactive flow.
[02:20] Owen: ok understood. for that SLA, the knobs are continuous batching threshold, max-concurrency per worker, and queue depth gating. and fallback to a smaller quantized model when queue depth > threshold.
[02:41] Maya: can you explain the fallback sequence again? Diego asked about model variant.
[02:46] Owen: yeah — primary is full fp16-ish model on RBX-32; fallback is a quantized RBX-16 variant we keep warm. routing policy routes to fallback when queueing latency estimate > 120ms or when node CPU/GPU saturates. it's fast to switch, about 200–400ms depending on KV rehydrate.
[03:05] Diego: KV rehydrate — I think that's where we saw a 300ms hit last time, was that right?
[03:09] Owen: approx, yes. if the fallback hasn't been used in a while, the KV cache for the fallback needs to rebuild, which can add overhead. we can pre-warm fallback in the lab.
[03:25] Priya: our SRE concern is burst behavior — if we automatically fallback, do we double the machine count? what's the cost pattern?
[03:33] Maya: good question, costs are a function of how we scale and how you configure burst capacity. we have reserved baseline and optional burst pools. Owen, maybe walk through the burst cost model briefly?
[03:45] Owen: sure. baseline reserved handles steady concurrency. burst uses short-lived instances where we accept a slightly higher per-token cost. for your target concurrency of 40 steady, we recommend small baseline plus a 20% burst buffer. pricing spreadsheet I sent earlier shows breakouts — Maya will attach again.
[04:04] Alex: (joins) sorry late — can someone share the p95 numbers again?
[04:08] Owen: sure, p95 sits around 900ms in production-ish run, p50 is 160ms. in our lab when we constrain concurrency to 20, p95 drops below 300ms.
[04:24] Sara: hmm. so the big gap is scaling from 20 to 40 concurrency. is that because batching saturates and then queueing grows?
[04:31] Owen: yes exactly. continuous batching increases GPU utilization but introduces variable per-request latency when queues back up. at low conc the batching amortizes token cost. at higher conc we see head-of-line issues if a large batch waits on a long prompt.
[04:52] Diego: what about request shaping? some of our calls send heavy context (8k tokens) and short prompts intermixed. can we instruct Redwood to split or route?
[05:03] Owen: we can policy route large-context requests to dedicated pathways — e.g., longer sequence workers with a different batching profile. that reduces noise for short prompts. There is a tradeoff: longer sequence workers have lower throughput so cost rises for long requests but they prevent tail effects on short-turn flows.
[05:24] Priya: can we see a recommended split? maybe 10% long, 90% short?
[05:29] Owen: from your traces it looked closer to 15% long. Diego, can you confirm?
[05:33] Diego: yeah our 48h sample looked like 13–17% long requests depending on time of day.
[05:40] Maya: so next step — Diego to upload trace and label long vs short requests. that helps Owen run targeted sweeps.
[05:50] Sara: agreed. also curious about queue shaping — you mentioned token-bucket shaping?
[05:55] Owen: yes, we have a queue-gate that uses token-bucket style admission. we can set burst tokens and refill rate to cap how many requests enter the GPU queue per second. that smooths arrival but increases client-side queueing.
[06:12] Alex: does client-side queueing show in our telemetry? we want to alert if client queueing exceeds X ms.
[06:18] Owen: we'll add client-queue-ms as a metric in the lab. currently you have server processing and GPU queue metrics; adding ingress queue timer is straightforward.
[06:29] Sara: perfect. about the lab — what's the plan and who needs to be present from our side?
[06:36] Liam: suggested lab agenda: pre-warm fallback behavior, batch/concurrency sweeps, routing split test for long-vs-short flows, and a stress run with synthetic spikes to verify fallback. we usually need an infra person to handle logs and occasional VPC peering tweaks.
[06:54] Diego: I'll be the infra person — I can do the peering and upload traces. Priya will own metrics collection.
[06:59] Maya: great. Owen what's the expected runtime for a full sweep?
[07:04] Owen: expect 3–4 hours for a comprehensive sweep (multiple concurrency points, each with warmup windows). but we can run a focused 90-minute smoke that covers the main knobs.
[07:17] Sara: we'd prefer the full sweep in the staging lab so results are reliable. can you do before 09/20?
[07:23] Owen: yes, we can do a full sweep the week of 09/20; earliest is 09/21 based on current lab slots.
[07:30] Priya: question on observability — will you provide trace-level mapping to our request IDs? we need to correlate end-user sessions.
[07:38] Maya: yes we can ingest your request IDs; Owen will add headers mapping. (aside) note that privacy redaction will be maintained per pilot terms.
[07:48] Owen: when you upload traces include X-Request-Id header mapping column, that makes correlation straightforward.
[07:55] Diego: ok we'll include that in the upload.
[08:00] Alex: one more on fallback: if fallback model returns lower quality, do you have automatic quality checks so we can avoid regressions?
[08:10] Owen: good point — we run a lightweight eval on a small prompt set during fallback to ensure the fallback doesn't diverge too far; if it does, we auto-throttle fallback and instead scale up baseline.
[08:24] Sara: can that eval be our prompt suite? we'd want to use our quality test set.
[08:29] Owen: absolutely — include your eval set in the drive and we'll run it as part of the lab.
[08:36] Maya: ok moving to pricing and contract notes — Maya: for pilot we usually include burst credits and a three-week lab allowance; after lab we roll to a month of steady traffic. I'll attach a pilot addendum.
[08:50] Diego: from compliance perspective, we need to confirm audit log retention and SSO SAML mapping. Priya will handle SOC2 questions.
[09:00] Priya: yes, SOC2 question — does Redwood provide per-request audit logs to our SIEM?
[09:05] Owen: yes we can stream audit logs to your endpoint or we can provide daily manifests. streaming requires a short setup.
[09:13] Priya: great, we'll prefer streaming to Splunk. I'll share endpoint details.
[09:18] Sara: any blockers on our side to get the lab data ready? Diego: timeline?
[09:23] Diego: I can get the 48h traces and a sample payload cover within 48 hours, so by 09/10. network peering window I need to confirm but likely 09/22 fits.
[09:34] Owen: perfect. technical detail: when we run the sweep we'll vary two main dims: batch threshold (0.5–3.0s wait window) and concurrency per worker (8, 16, 24, 32, 40). we'll log p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, and per-request queue wait.
[09:53] Maya: that's helpful. for your expected targets remind us: you want p50 <200 and p95 <800 right?
[09:59] Sara: yes that's the customer target. ideally p95 <500 but we'll accept 800 at pilot stage.
[10:08] Owen: ok note added. two more things — we recommend enabling prefix caching for multi-turn heavy users, and setting a TTL of 10 minutes for their KV cache during pilot to improve warm-hit rates.
[10:22] Diego: will that increase memory usage dramatically?
[10:25] Owen: modestly, but within our recommended instance sizes. we'll show memory and GPU memory usage per config in the CSV.
[10:36] Priya: are there any known regressions with quantized RBX-16 vs fp16 that we should pre-watch?
[10:42] Owen: in some rare samplings, RBX-16 has slightly altered tokenization boundary effects leading to punctuation variance; we track rouge-like deltas on the eval set. we'll flag any prompt examples where delta > threshold.
[10:58] Alex: can we automate daily checks during pilot for quality drift?
[11:03] Owen: yes, Redwood Optimize can run daily evals and send regression alerts; for pilot we can set a lenient threshold and adjust.
[11:14] Maya: ok recap before we wrap: 1) Diego uploads traces + sample payloads by 09/10 2) Owen runs batch/concurrency sweep and shares results by 09/13 3) Maya sends pilot addendum and pricing by 09/11 4) schedule lab week of 09/20 — target 09/21 for full sweep 5) Priya provides Splunk endpoint for audit logs streaming by 09/12.
[11:40] Sara: that matches our notes. any other risks? Alex: we worry about fallback quality and cost.
[11:48] Owen: we'll quantify quality delta and cost delta in the CSV; if fallback quality is bad we won't enable auto-fallback without your signoff.
[11:58] Diego: also can you show us a model of cost per 1M tokens with and without burst? that helps procurement.
[12:05] Maya: yes that's in the pricing sheet I'll attach.
[12:12] Priya: final — alerting thresholds, can we get sample Grafana dashboard?
[12:17] Owen: yes we'll share a Grafana starter template and a telemetry mapping doc.
[12:23] Maya: ok last minute logistics — any blocking security requirements for the lab?
[12:29] Priya: only the standard SAML + IP allowlist plus single subnet peering; Diego will confirm details.
[12:36] Sara: thanks everyone. Maya, can you send calendar invite for lab week once dates locked?
[12:41] Maya: will do. Owen, any final technical caveat?
[12:44] Owen: just that some runs will require warmup windows of 15–30 minutes to reach steady-state; please plan the lab slot accordingly.
[12:54] Maya: perfect, thanks all. closing notes: we will reconvene after sweep to review CSV and decide rollout.
[13:03] Sara: thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
